mainTopic: How רבי יהושע's two rulings (his tradition vs. his own reasoning) differ, and the practical difference between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע: whether milk (חלב) proves an animal already gave birth (פטור from בכורה).
overview: The amud opens by finishing the explanation of why רבי יהושע ruled one way by his tradition (לגמריה) and another way by his own reasoning (לסבריה) about a young goat that had a discharge. One explanation is that they disagree whether an animal can give birth after incomplete months (יולדת למקוטעין). The other is that they disagree whether part of a day counts as a whole day (מקצת היום ככולו). The גמרא then quotes רבי עקיבא, who rejects calculations and rules only by what is known, and asks what practical difference there is between him and רבי יהושע. רבי חנינא מסורא answers that they disagree whether milk (חלב) proves an animal already gave birth, which would exempt its next baby from בכורה. The גמרא challenges this from a משנה in יבמות, where רבי יהושע does not worry about a minority (מיעוט). It therefore reverses the opinions (איפוך): רבי יהושע says milk exempts, and a ברייתא confirms this. Finally, a new ברייתא describes a young goat whose daughters and granddaughters became enough for מעשר בהמה within one year. The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed each daughter to have three babies, and why it did not let the mother give birth again.

steps.title: First explanation: they argue whether an animal can give birth after incomplete months
steps.stepSummary: According to רבי יהושע's tradition, we do not say an animal can give birth after incomplete months. According to his own reasoning, we do say it.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to what he received from his teachers, we do not say that an animal can give birth after incomplete months. According to his own reasoning, we do say that an animal can give birth after incomplete months.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי יהושע's received tradition and his personal reasoning reach different rulings about the goat. The difference is whether a pregnancy can be shorter than the full count of months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the tradition (לגמריה), a pregnancy must be complete. A goat that gave birth within its first year must therefore have become pregnant soon after the discharge, so the discharge was not a fetus and the next baby is still a בכור. According to his own reasoning (לסבריה), a pregnancy can be cut short. The pregnancy could then have started later, the discharge could have been a fetus, and the next baby is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: According to his tradition (what he learned from his teachers)
We say / we apply the principle

steps.confusionAlert: לגמריה does not mean 'completely.' Here it comes from גמרא in the sense of 'learned tradition,' meaning what רבי יהושע heard from his teachers. Do not confuse it with לגמרי ('entirely').

phrases.english: According to his tradition — we do not say
phrases.notes: His received teaching from his teachers

phrases.english: that it gives birth after incomplete months;
phrases.notes: A pregnancy must run its full term

phrases.english: according to his own reasoning — we do say
phrases.notes: His personal logic

phrases.english: that it gives birth after incomplete months.
phrases.notes: A shorter pregnancy is possible, so the discharge may have been a real fetus

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues earlier by answering how רבי יהושע's tradition and reasoning differ.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the underlying point of disagreement between רבי יהושע's tradition and his own reasoning?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree whether an animal can give birth after incomplete months (יולדת למקוטעין).

steps.title: Second explanation: they argue whether part of a day counts as a whole day
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, both sides agree that a pregnancy cannot be cut short. The real dispute is whether part of a day counts as a whole day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you wish, say: we do not say that an animal gives birth after incomplete months. Here they disagree about whether part of the day counts like the whole day. According to his own reasoning, we say part of the day counts like the whole day. According to his tradition, we do not say part of the day counts like the whole day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different explanation of the same dispute. It keeps the rule that pregnancies are never short and moves the argument to how days are counted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If part of a day counts as a whole day (מקצת היום ככולו), the goat could have become pregnant on the thirtieth day after the discharge and still give birth just before the year ends. That is רבי יהושע's own reasoning. If part of a day does not count, the earliest possible birth falls into the second year. That is his tradition.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative answer)
Part of the day is like the whole day

steps.confusionAlert: Notice that the sides are reversed in wording order. This time לסבריה (his reasoning) is mentioned first and לגמריה (his tradition) second. The outcome still matches step 1: his reasoning is the lenient side that allows the discharge to exempt the next baby.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
phrases.notes: Signals an alternative explanation

phrases.english: we do not say that it gives birth (after incomplete months),
phrases.notes: Both sides now agree on this point

phrases.english: and here they disagree about whether part of the day is like the whole day.
phrases.notes: The new point of dispute

phrases.english: According to his own reasoning — we say part of the day is like the whole day;
phrases.notes: So a birth just before the year ends is possible

phrases.aramaic: לִגְמָרֵיהּ — לָא אָמְרִינַן מִקְצָת הַיּוֹם כְּכוּלּוֹ.
phrases.english: according to his tradition — we do not say part of the day is like the whole day.
phrases.notes: So the earliest birth falls in the second year

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain רבי יהושע's split ruling: (1) יולדת למקוטעין, or (2) מקצת היום ככולו. Either way, his own reasoning is the side that lets the discharge exempt the next baby.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, alternative explanation of the same dispute addressed in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the underlying point of disagreement between רבי יהושע's tradition and his own reasoning?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Everyone agrees there are no premature births. They disagree whether מקצת היום ככולו.

steps.title: Quoting רבי עקיבא's different approach from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the ברייתא. There רבי עקיבא rejects רבי יהושע's method of calculating and gives his own rule based on what is known.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said: I have not come to this method. Rather, anything that is known (to have given birth, the כהן gets nothing here), and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on and quotes רבי עקיבא's statement from the ברייתא. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא does not rely on calculations of ages and pregnancy lengths. He says that if it is known the animal gave birth, there is no בכור. If it is known it did not give birth, the next baby goes to the כהן. If it is uncertain, the owner may eat it once it has a blemish.

keyTerms.meaning: I did not come to (adopt) this method
Etc. (the quote continues; see the full ברייתא)

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said:
phrases.notes: Quoting the ברייתא

phrases.aramaic: אֲנִי לֹא בָּאתִי לִידֵי מִדָּה זוֹ,
phrases.english: I have not come to this method,
phrases.notes: He rejects calculating by ages and timelines

phrases.english: rather, anything that is known, etc.
phrases.notes: Known birth means no בכור; known non-birth means a בכור; uncertain means it is eaten with a blemish

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: אֲנִי לֹא בָּאתִי לִידֵי מִדָּה זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the same ברייתא, which gives רבי עקיבא's response to רבי יהושע's calculation method.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא rules by what is known: known birth means exempt, known non-birth means a בכור, and doubt means it is eaten once blemished.

steps.title: What practical difference is there between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in what real case רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע would actually rule differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference is there between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. Their approaches sound different, but where would the actual ruling change? This sets up רבי חנינא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both rabbis seem to say that if we don't know, the animal is a doubtful בכור. So the גמרא wants a concrete case where the two methods give different results.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ?
phrases.english: What is there (in practice) between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua?
phrases.notes: A request for the practical difference

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the practical meaning of the רבי עקיבא quote in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete case in which רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע would rule differently.

steps.title: The difference is whether milk proves the animal already gave birth
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא מסורא says they disagree about an animal producing milk. רבי עקיבא follows the majority, and most animals produce milk only after giving birth, so the next baby is exempt. רבי יהושע is concerned about the minority that produce milk without giving birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא of Sura said: The difference between them is whether milk exempts. רבי עקיבא holds that milk exempts: follow the majority of animals, and most animals do not produce milk unless they have given birth. רבי יהושע holds: there is a minority that produce milk even though they have not given birth.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא answers the question. The practical difference is an animal that already has milk: does that prove it gave birth before, so its next baby is not a בכור?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא relies on רוב (majority). Since most milk-producing animals have given birth, he treats this one as having given birth, and the next baby is exempt. רבי יהושע takes the מיעוט (minority) into account. Some animals produce milk without giving birth, so the next baby remains a doubtful בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: Milk exempts (the next baby from בכורה)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי חנינא מסורא's practical difference between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע is חלב פוטר: does milk prove a previous birth? Do not memorize who holds which side yet. The גמרא challenges this version in Steps 6-7 and reverses the opinions in Step 8. In the final version, רבי יהושע says milk exempts and רבי עקיבא says it does not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic example of the larger question of how far we rely on רוב versus worrying about a מיעוט in cases of doubt.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina of Sura said:
phrases.notes: He answers the question

phrases.english: Whether milk exempts — that is the difference between them.
phrases.notes: Case: the animal already has milk

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva holds: milk exempts,
phrases.notes: The next baby is not a בכור

phrases.english: follow the majority of animals,
phrases.notes: Reliance on רוב

phrases.english: and the majority of animals do not produce milk
unless they have given birth.
phrases.notes: So milk indicates a previous birth

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds:
but there is a minority that produce milk
phrases.notes: Concern for the מיעוט

phrases.english: even though they have not given birth.
phrases.notes: So the next baby is a doubtful בכור

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא מִסּוּרָא: חָלָב פּוֹטֵר אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete case in which רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע would rule differently.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An animal producing milk: רבי עקיבא exempts its next baby based on רוב, and רבי יהושע considers the מיעוט, so the baby is a doubtful בכור.

steps.title: Does רבי יהושע really worry about a minority?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 5. It quotes a משנה in יבמות where רבי יהושע says a woman does not need to worry that her pregnant mother-in-law gave birth to a boy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יהושע really worry about a minority? But we learned in a משנה: If she has a mother-in-law who went overseas, she does not need to worry. If the mother-in-law left while pregnant, she does need to worry. רבי יהושע says: she does not need to worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 5, which said that רבי יהושע worries about the minority of animals that give milk without giving birth. It quotes a משנה that seems to show the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case: a woman's husband died with no children. If a brother-in-law exists, she needs יבום or חליצה. Her mother-in-law left the country while pregnant and might have had a boy, who would be a brother-in-law. The first opinion says the woman must worry about this, but רבי יהושע says she does not. The reason will be explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Does he really worry about? (the opening of a challenge)
But we learned in a משנה
She must worry, she has to take the possibility into account

steps.confusionAlert: The woman here is the daughter-in-law, not the mother-in-law. The worry is that the mother-in-law gave birth to a boy, who would be a brother-in-law (יבם). That would stop the widow from remarrying without יבום or חליצה.

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Yehoshua really worry about a minority?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתְנַן: הָיְתָה לָהּ חֲמוֹת — אֵינָהּ חוֹשֶׁשֶׁת,
phrases.english: But we learned: if she had a mother-in-law (who went overseas), she does not need to worry;
phrases.notes: From the משנה in יבמות 119a.

phrases.english: if she left while full (pregnant), she must worry.
phrases.notes: The worry is that a son was born, who could perform יבום.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says: she does not need to worry.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי חָיֵישׁ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְמִיעוּט? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חנינא מסורא's explanation in Step 5, which had רבי יהושע worrying about a minority.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 5 that רבי יהושע worries about the minority of animals that give milk without giving birth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the משנה in יבמות, רבי יהושע ignores a possibility that is only a minority. So he should not worry about a minority in the milk case either.

steps.title: Why רבי יהושע ignores the chance that a boy was born
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבי יהושע's reasoning in the יבמות case. Boys are a minority of all pregnancies, and he does not worry about a minority. This completes the challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we said: What is רבי יהושע's reason? He holds that most pregnant women give birth and a minority miscarry. Of all those who give birth, half have boys and half have girls. Add the minority who miscarry to the half who have girls. Then boys are a minority, and we do not worry about a minority!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge by recalling the known reason for רבי יהושע's view. It shows clearly that he does not worry about a minority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Start with all pregnancies. A few end in miscarriage, and of the births, half are girls. Put the miscarriages together with the girls, and the boys become less than half. So רבי יהושע ignores the chance of a boy because it is a minority. This contradicts Step 5, where he worried about a minority.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not worry about it

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the גמרא combines groups to decide what is a majority and what is a minority. The same reasoning is used in other places in ש"ס.

phrases.english: And we said: what is the reason of Rabbi Yehoshua?
He holds: most pregnant women give birth,
and a minority miscarry,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל הַיּוֹלְדוֹת — מֶחֱצָה זְכָרִים וּמֶחֱצָה נְקֵבוֹת.
phrases.english: and of all who give birth, half have males and half have females.
Combine the minority who miscarry with the half who have females,
and the males become a minority,
and we do not worry about a minority!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge from Step 6 by showing exactly why רבי יהושע's view means he ignores a minority.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 5's claim that רבי יהושע worries about a minority.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהושע's own reason in יבמות is 'we do not worry about a minority.' That openly contradicts Step 5.

steps.title: Switch the two opinions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the opinions in the milk dispute should be reversed. רבי יהושע is the one who follows the majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by switching who says what. Now רבי יהושע follows the majority and רבי עקיבא worries about the minority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי יהושע does not worry about a minority, he must be the one who says milk exempts, because most animals give milk only after giving birth. רבי עקיבא is the one who worries about the minority that give milk without giving birth. The next step brings support for this switch.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not keep Step 5's version in mind. After this answer, רבי יהושע says milk exempts and רבי עקיבא says it does not.

phrases.english: Rather, reverse (the opinions);

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from Steps 6-7 by switching the speakers in Step 5's dispute.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא follows the majority and רבי יהושע worries about the minority, so for רבי יהושע milk does not exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהושע follows the majority, so milk exempts. רבי עקיבא worries about the minority, so milk does not exempt.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the switched version
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that has the opinions in the reversed order: רבי יהושע says milk exempts, and רבי עקיבא says it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it is taught in a ברייתא: Milk exempts. These are the words of רבי יהושע. רבי עקיבא says: Milk does not exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the reversed version is not just a guess. A ברייתא actually teaches it that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Milk exempts' means that if an animal gave milk, we assume it already gave birth. So its next baby is not a בכור. This fits רבי יהושע following the majority. רבי עקיבא worries about the minority that give milk without having given birth, so for him the next baby may still be a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it is taught in a ברייתא
Exempts (the next baby from being a בכור)

steps.whatToRemember: Final version: רבי יהושע says milk exempts (he follows the majority). רבי עקיבא says milk does not exempt (he worries about the minority). This fits רבי יהושע's view in יבמות that we do not worry about a minority.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: חָלָב פּוֹטֵר, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ.
phrases.english: And so it is taught: milk exempts; these are the words of Rabbi Yehoshua.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: חָלָב אֵינוֹ פּוֹטֵר.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: milk does not exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: חָלָב פּוֹטֵר, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reversal from Step 8 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The reversed attribution: רבי יהושע says milk exempts.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that teaches 'חלב פוטר, דברי רבי יהושע; רבי עקיבא אומר חלב אינו פוטר.'

steps.title: A young goat whose family needed מעשר within one year
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: a young goat had three daughters, and each daughter had three babies. All of them enter the pen to be tithed. רבי שמעון says he saw this happen within the goat's first year.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: A young goat gave birth to three daughters, and each of her daughters gave birth to three. All of them enter the pen to be tithed. רבי שמעון said: I saw a goat whose offspring needed tithing within its own year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a ברייתא. It shows how fast goats can give birth, so fast that a goat born this year can produce enough offspring for מעשר בהמה in the same year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעשר בהמה applies only when there are at least ten animals born in the same year. Here the young goat had 3 daughters, and they had 3 each (9 more), so there are more than ten. This means a goat can give birth very young, and her daughters can also give birth, all within one year. רבי שמעון says he saw this himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Pen, the enclosure where animals are counted for tithing
Within its year, its first year of life

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how quickly goats give birth. This matters for the סוגיא's discussion of how soon an animal can give birth again.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: גְּדִיָּיה שֶׁיָּלְדָה שָׁלֹשׁ בָּנוֹת,
phrases.english: The Sages taught: a young goat that gave birth to three daughters,
and all her daughters each gave birth to three —
all of them enter the pen to be tithed.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: אֲנִי רָאִיתִי שֶׁעִישְּׂרָה בְּתוֹךְ שְׁנָתָהּ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said: I saw (a goat) whose offspring were tithed within its year.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: גְּדִיָּיה שֶׁיָּלְדָה שָׁלֹשׁ בָּנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא on a related topic: how quickly goats give birth.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A goat and her daughters can produce enough offspring within one year to be counted together for מעשר בהמה.

steps.title: Why does each daughter need three babies?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא says each daughter had three. Ten animals would be reached if one daughter had three and the other two had two each.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need it to teach 'three each'? Let one of them give birth to three, and the others two each!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the exact wording of the ברייתא. Fewer babies would already be enough for ten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Count it: 3 daughters + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10, which is already the minimum for מעשר. So why does the ברייתא describe 3 babies from every daughter, which gives 12? The גמרא is pointing to wording that seems more than needed. The answer comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it to teach?

phrases.english: Why do I need it to teach 'three each'?
Let one of them give birth to three,
and the others two each!
phrases.notes: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10, the minimum for מעשר בהמה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא quoted in Step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the ברייתא describes three babies from each daughter, when fewer would already reach ten for מעשר.

steps.title: One daughter needs three, so the ברייתא says three for all
steps.stepSummary: Because at least one daughter had to have three babies to reach ten, the ברייתא simply said all of them had three.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since there is one daughter that could not be enough unless she had three, the ברייתא taught that all of them gave birth to three each.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 11. One daughter really did need to have three, so the ברייתא used 'three each' for all of them to keep the wording simple.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Count the animals. If all three daughters had only two babies, you get 3 daughters + 6 babies = 9, which is short of ten. So one daughter must have three (3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10). Once 'three' had to be mentioned for one daughter, the ברייתא said it about all of them, even though it was only needed for one.

keyTerms.meaning: Since / because (it was already saying one thing, it said the same for the rest)

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not claiming the extra babies are needed. Only one daughter actually needed three. The others are described as having three only to keep the wording consistent.

phrases.notes: Without her having three babies, the total would only reach nine

steps.triggerLanguage: אַיְּידֵי דְּאִיכָּא חֲדָא דְּלָא סַגִּיא בְּלָא שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question in Step 11 about why each daughter is said to have had three.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One daughter must have three to reach ten. Because of her, the ברייתא used 'three' for all of them to keep the wording consistent (an אַיְּידֵי explanation).

steps.title: Why mention three at all, if the mother could give birth again?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed any daughter to have three. All daughters could have had two, and the mother could have given birth again to reach ten.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why do I need to teach 'three' at all? Let all of them give birth to two, and let her, the mother, give birth again together with them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further and asks why the ברייתא mentioned 'three' at all. This question sets up the next move: learning something from the fact that the ברייתא did not choose this simpler case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other way to reach ten is 3 daughters + 6 babies (two each) + 1 new baby from the original mother = 10. With that count, no goat ever needs to have three at once. Since the ברייתא avoided this option, the גמרא is hinting that a goat cannot give birth again within the same year.

keyTerms.meaning: And let her go back / do it again

steps.confusionAlert: 'אִיהִי' (her) means the original young goat, the mother of the three daughters. It does not mean one of the daughters.
steps.whyThisMatters: This question is the basis for an inference about animal biology that matters for counting animals for מעשר בהמה: the ברייתא's wording suggests a goat does not give birth twice in the same year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 12's answer by asking why 'three' is needed at all, since there is another way to reach ten.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the ברייתא did not use the simpler case where every daughter had two and the original mother gave birth again. The implied conclusion is that a goat cannot give birth twice in one year.
